mcqs.question: What core weakness in Linux's older O(1) scheduler did CFS specifically address?
options: The O(1) scheduler ran only on single-core machines
The O(1) scheduler had no concept of process priority at all
It was slower asymptotically than every possible alternative design
It relied on heuristic interactivity detection that was fragile and had known misjudgment cases, versus CFS's principled fairness invariant
mcqs.explanation: CFS's design deliberately replaced heuristic guessing (which sometimes misjudged workloads) with a mathematically clean, always-applicable fairness rule. The old scheduler wasn't single-core-only, did have priority concepts, and "slower than every alternative" isn't the actual motivation cited for the change.

mcqs.question: What is CFS's single scheduling rule, in terms of vruntime?
options: Run whichever task has consumed the least real (wall-clock) CPU time so far, unweighted
Always run the task with the smallest vruntime among runnable tasks
Run tasks strictly in the order they became runnable, like FCFS
Run whichever task has the highest nice value numerically
mcqs.explanation: CFS's entire decision procedure reduces to picking the smallest-vruntime runnable task, where vruntime already incorporates weighting from nice value — it isn't raw unweighted CPU time, isn't FCFS-style arrival order, and a higher nice value means lower weight/priority, not higher.

mcqs.question: Under CFS, what does setting a task's nice value to -20 actually do?
options: It moves the task into a completely separate real-time scheduling class
It guarantees the task always runs before any other task, with zero exceptions
It increases the task's weight so its vruntime accumulates more slowly, letting it be scheduled more often and get a larger proportional CPU share
It has no measurable effect under CFS, only under the older O(1) scheduler
mcqs.explanation: Nice value under CFS is a weight multiplier affecting how fast vruntime grows, giving proportionally more CPU share, not an absolute guarantee or a class change — real-time classes are entirely separate from nice-based CFS priority. It has a real, measurable effect, not none.

mcqs.question: Why does CFS need far fewer tunable parameters than MLFQ to achieve a similar goal?
options: CFS doesn't actually achieve MLFQ's goal at all, it optimizes for something unrelated
MLFQ's behavior is entirely hard-coded with no parameters, unlike CFS
CFS's single vruntime-ordering invariant produces the interactive-favoring, starvation-resistant behavior as a mathematical side effect, without needing separate queues, quanta, or boost intervals
CFS uses machine learning to automatically tune itself, unlike MLFQ
mcqs.explanation: CFS's one rule (least vruntime runs next) naturally produces MLFQ-like behavior for I/O-bound and CPU-bound tasks without any of MLFQ's separate mechanisms each needing their own tuning. It does target the same behavioral goal, MLFQ does have real tunable parameters, and CFS doesn't use machine learning.

mcqs.question: Why doesn't setting nice -20 on a Linux process give it real-time-like latency guarantees?
options: It's still a task in the normal CFS class, subject to the fairness invariant and sharing the CPU proportionally, with no formal worst-case latency bound
Nice -20 is not a valid value on modern Linux systems
Nice -20 actually reduces the task's CPU share instead of increasing it
Nice values only take effect after a system reboot
mcqs.explanation: Nice -20 is a strong preference within CFS's fairness model, not a move into a formally-guaranteed real-time class — for that, a task needs SCHED_FIFO/SCHED_RR or SCHED_DEADLINE instead. Nice -20 is valid and does increase share (not decrease it), and it takes effect immediately, no reboot needed.

mcqs.question: A Kubernetes pod has a generous CPU request but is still observed being throttled under load. What's a likely explanation grounded in how CFS-based CPU allocation works?
options: CPU requests are hard reservations in Kubernetes, so throttling under a generous request should be impossible
The pod is hitting a CFS bandwidth quota (a hard limit) or losing the proportional-fairness contest for shares under contention, since requests map to proportional weight, not a guarantee
Kubernetes does not use CFS or cgroups for CPU allocation at all
Throttling only happens due to network bandwidth limits, never CPU scheduling
mcqs.explanation: CPU requests translate to CFS-honored proportional shares, not hard reservations, so contention can still throttle a pod with a generous request — and a separately configured hard limit uses CFS bandwidth control, a distinct quota mechanism. Requests aren't hard reservations, Kubernetes does rely on cgroups/CFS, and this scenario is about CPU, not network, throttling.
